content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Define endothermic reactions in terms of energy transfer
Identify common types of endothermic reactions
Draw and interpret energy level diagrams for endothermic reactions
Describe practical applications of endothermic reactions
absorb energy from the surroundings, usually as heat. They are less common than exothermic reactions but have important applications, including cold packs and photosynthesis.
Energy required to break old bonds > Energy released by forming new bonds
Net energy is absorbed from the surroundings

Certain salts absorb heat when dissolving:
Ammonium nitrate makes water very cold
Not all dissolving is endothermic (NaOH is exothermic)
Energy is stored in the products

Contains ammonium nitrate and water (separated by barrier)
Used for sports injuries, first aid
Contains citric acid and sodium bicarbonate
When saliva dissolves them, they react
Endothermic reaction creates cold, fizzy sensation
Thermal decomposition used to make quicklime (CaO)
The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate absorbs 178 kJ per mole. Write the thermochemical equation.
Draw an energy level diagram for the decomposition of limestone (ΔH = +178 kJ/mol).

Energy
   ↑

A student dissolves ammonium chloride in water. The beaker becomes cold. Explain this observation.
The dissolving of ammonium chloride is endothermic
Energy is absorbed from the surroundings (the water and beaker)
The surroundings lose energy and get colder
This makes the beaker feel cold to touch
Explain why photosynthesis is classified as endothermic.
Photosynthesis absorbs light energy from the sun
This energy is used to break bonds in CO₂ and H₂O
The energy is stored in the bonds of glucose
Products (glucose) have more energy than reactants
Energy is absorbed, so the reaction is endothermic
Suggest why thermal decomposition reactions stop when heating is stopped.
Energy must be continuously supplied for the reaction to continue
When heating stops, no more energy is supplied
Without energy input, the reaction cannot proceed
Some dissolving is exothermic (e.g., NaOH, CaCl₂)
Drawing energy diagram with products below reactants
For endothermic, products are HIGHER (more energy)
Writing ΔH as negative for endothermic
ΔH is always POSITIVE for endothermic reactions

A student mixes citric acid with sodium hydrogen carbonate in a beaker. The temperature drops from 22°C to 14°C.
a) Calculate the temperature change. (1 mark)
b) Is this reaction exothermic or endothermic? (1 mark)
c) Explain your answer to part (b). (2 marks)
A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings
Breaking down a compound using heat
The process plants use to make glucose using light energy
A device that uses an endothermic reaction to cool
Common examples: thermal decomposition, photosynthesis, some dissolving
Require continuous energy input (e.g., heating, light)
